rv.q: This is a stunning, richly textured piece of work, both particular and universal.
Tinuke Craig’s beautifully realised production creates a microcosm of defiance and dashed dreams.
Wondrous and captivating, Craig’s production gets this play’s soul.
Male bravado is the downfall of these men, Craig's production playing with ideas of masculinity without ever feeling preachy.
It is a pity that in Tinuke Craig’s intermittently lively and sometimes indistinct production, Alex Lowde’s design is flat.
Jitney is a triumph of hard work and passion from all creatives involved and that will reflect in every standing ovation the show will inevitably receive.
It's a fine production of a fascinating play.

Another reason to celebrate is Tinuke Craig’s terrific production at the Old Vic (produced with Leeds Playhouse and Headlong), which gives Jitney an energy and sense of wider perspective that the play, concentrated as it is around a single interior, often appears to lack.

This final revision, whilst imperfect, stands as a testament to a writer whose canon provides a fascinating insight into a section of society whose uniqueness and rich complexity has long been undervalued and under-represented.
Jitney is very much worth the ride.

While it lacks the power of later plays such as Fences and Joe Turner's Come And Gone, it is an engaging and busy ensemble piece fleshed out by characterful performances.

cn.t: Critics praise Tinuke Craig's vivid revival of Wilson's early work, calling it a masterclass in character study that powerfully captures Black working-class life in 1970s Pittsburgh, though one dissenter finds it plodding and overlong.
